newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund futures surge as reserve debate resolved.
newsitem.headline: Bund futures surge as reserve debate resolved.

text.p: Bund futures staged an impressive rally on Tuesday as traders took heart from a deal struck between the Bundesbank and Finance Ministry over revaluing the Bundesbank's official reserves.
The DTB June Bund future was up 65 basis points late in the day at 101.45, near its highest level of the day.
The benchmark cash 10-year Bund climbed to 101.11 from 100.65 to yield 5.84 percent.
Under the compromise, the Bundesbank and the government agreed to revalue gold and currency reserves at the end of 1997, but would only transfer the profits to Bonn in 1998.
Bonn had originally sought to have profits stemming from the revaluation transfered to the government this year, providing funds to pay down debt.
The deal eased fears that Germany would engage in "creative accounting" to meet Maastricht Treaty deficit criteria, reassuring debt markets.

It once again, however, opened the question of how Germany would close its budget gap and raised worries that Bonn might try to enter EMU with a deficit slightly higher than the three percent of gross domestic product level stipulated by Maastricht.
Traders said that once the market had finished celebrating the gold deal, profit-taking could set in, especially on the long-end of the curve.
"The market fear over the longer term is that we will get a soft euro and bond yields could go up," one bond analyst said.
Several said the 101.40 level was especially important and a sustained break of that level would pave the way for the market to fall back toward 101.90.
"In view of the long-term interest rate outlook, the gains seem to be a bit over done, but we should be able to hold around 101.00," one trader said.
Resolution of the German reserve fight helped Bunds climb against U.S. debt with the spread between 10-year maturities climbing to 111 basis points from 108 basis points at the close on Monday.
The yield curve, meanwhile, flattened by four basis points to 230 basis points between two- and 10-year maturities.
Although details of how Bonn will cover its budget gap will dominate the market, traders said German industrial production data due as early as Wednesday could create some volatility.
German unemployment data, due Friday, would otherwise be the next major domestic event.
